l2_text:
**The knowers are one, and the one is the Lord**

The jñānādhikāra — the whole first adhikāra of the Īśvarapratyabhijñāvivṛtivimarśinī — comes to its
close. And it closes, fittingly, on the unity. It was said at the start that the one is the maheśvara;
now the unity is established. Kārikā 10: without that unity, the world-path of the consciousnesses
would not be; from the manifestation-unity, that one-ness, that one alone is the knower, it is
established.

The argument is simple and decisive. The whole dealing of the world — the path by which consciousnesses
know, remember, and act together — would be impossible if the consciousnesses were a scattered crowd of
mutually opaque streams. But the dealing is; so the consciousnesses must be one. And this is not hard to
accept, for the manifestation (prakāśa) is the very essence of the consciousnesses, and the
manifestation is one — there is no difference in the light itself. That one manifestation is, in truth,
the knower. The one light that shines in all the consciousnesses is the one knower, the param-essence
knower, the paramātman. Even the Sāṃkhya's and the Jaiminīya's self-luminous consciousness, and the
ancient Vaiśeṣika's consciousness-nature self, all point to this one.

The objection comes: "each cognition rests, in its own self-experience, in its own joining — what is
new here?" And the answer is that the known itself — the blue and the rest — has the manifestation as
its param-essence; the blue is, in its being, the light. So the unity is real, not a construction. And
the apparent difference of the known is made only by the māyā-power: the known-marker part, made
distinct from the manifestation as if it were other, is still the manifestation's own part. The
difference is the māyā's making; the unity is the truth.

And the Sāṃkhya's puruṣa — the separate self it posits — is not another at all. It is the un-recognized
own-lordship, the contracted consciousness; its knowledge and action, dealt as "I," are the
"I"-recollection. And this "I"-recollection, Abhinavagupta notes, is the pervader of all the states —
the pure, the mixed, the un-pure — gathered, not abandoned. The threefold self-recognition runs through
them all.

Then kārikā 11 sums up the whole: he alone, by the fixed reflexive-awareness-ness, is the great Lord;
the reflexive-awareness alone, of the God, in the pure knowledge-action, since. The great-Lordship is
nothing but the reflexive-awareness — the one who is aware of himself, fixedly, is the Lord; and that
reflexive-awareness is the God's own pure knowledge-and-action. The great-Lordship is not an added
power; it is the self-awareness itself, the "I" that knows and acts, the one knower.

And so the jñānādhikāra — the adhikāra on knowledge — is complete. The ||8|| colophon closes the
vimarśa on the great-Lordship in the one-support of the powers; and the great colophon reads:
"completed — this, the first jñānādhikāra." The first of the four adhikāras of the IPVV is done. It
has established the self, the powers, the one knower, the great-Lordship — all culminating in the
unity: the one manifestation is the one knower, and the one knower, aware of himself, is the Lord.

---

c1.body:
> The passage closes the jñānādhikāra with the unity of the knowers. Kārikā 10: the whole dealing of
> the world — the path by which consciousnesses know, remember, and act together — would be impossible
> if the consciousnesses were mutually opaque streams; but the dealing is, so the consciousnesses must
> be one. The unity is argued via the dealing, not by a bare assertion of identity. The Sāṃkhya's
> separate puruṣa is then re-read: it is not another self but the un-recognized own-lordship, the
> contracted consciousness.
>
> Kārikā 11 draws the conclusion: the great-Lordship is nothing but the reflexive awareness. The
> Lordship is not a fifth power added to the four; it is what the four are. The powers reduce to the
> self-awareness, and the self-awareness is the Lord.
>
> The passage argues the unity via the dealing and identifies the Lordship with the self-awareness. It
> does not by itself establish the identity of all supports by the felt alone; that is a further claim.

c1_source.summary:
Kārikā 10: without the unity of the knowers, the world-path of the consciousnesses would not be; from
the manifestation-unity, that one alone is the knower, it is established. The whole dealing of the
world would be impossible if the consciousnesses were mutually opaque streams; but the dealing is, so
the consciousnesses must be one. Kārikā 11: the great-Lordship is nothing but the reflexive-awareness —
the one who is aware of himself, fixedly, is the Lord. The great-Lordship is not an added power; it is
the self-awareness itself.
c1_source.function:
The passage closes the jñānādhikāra. It argues the unity of the knowers (kārikā 10) and identifies the
great-Lordship with the reflexive-awareness (kārikā 11), completing the account of the powers.
c1_source.key_terms:
- **the unity (kārikā 10)** — the one manifestation; the one knower.
- **the dealing (vyavahāra)** — the world-path of knowing/remembering/acting together.
- **the māheśvarya (kārikā 11)** — the great-Lordship, identified with the reflexive-awareness.
- **the puruṣa** — the Sāṃkhya's separate self, re-read as the un-recognized own-lordship.
c1_source.local_context:
This closes the aṣṭamo vimarśa and the whole jñānādhikāra. It follows the one-support (V2-O) and its
proof (V2-P, V2-Q); it is the culmination.
c1_source.explanation:
The unity-argument is argued via the dealing, not by a bare assertion of identity. The world-path of
knowing, remembering, and acting together would be impossible if the consciousnesses were a scattered
crowd of mutually opaque streams; but the dealing is; so they must be one — the one manifestation. The
Sāṃkhya's separate puruṣa is then re-read: it is not another self but the un-recognized own-lordship,
the contracted consciousness.

Kārikā 11 draws the conclusion: the great-Lordship is the reflexive-awareness. The Lordship is not a
fifth power added to the four; it is what the four are. The powers reduce to the self-awareness, and the
self-awareness is the Lord.
c1_source.boundary_/_open:
The passage argues the unity via the dealing and identifies the Lordship with the self-awareness. It
does not by itself establish the numerical identity of all supports by the felt alone; that identity is
a further claim. The Sāṃkhya/Jaiminīya/Vaiśeṣika (1.2.7) references are cited; their exact frames
remain open.
c1_source.related_passages:
- **V2-O** — the one-support, the transcendental argument.
- **V2-P/Q** — the proof of the one knower.
- **IPK 1.5.11** — the reflexivity at the root.
